item.title: Endpoint-specific mortality associated with malignancy among adults with sepsis or septic shock: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description: Sepsis is a major global health challenge and increasingly affects patients with complex conditions such as malignancy. Prior studies suggest higher mortality in this population, but interpretation is limited by aggregation of heterogeneous endpoints. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to clarify endpoint-specific prognostic associations between malignancy and mortality in adults with sepsis or septic shock. item.title: Intensive Care Unit Management of the Hemodynamically Significant Pulmonary Embolism.
item.description: This article reviews ICU management of hemodynamically significant pulmonary embolism. It highlights that patients with right‑ventricular failure, hemodynamic instability, or cardiac arrest require advanced monitoring and intervention. Key points include rapid diagnosis, risk stratification, timely reperfusion, and tailored hemodynamic and respiratory support.

item.description: Advances in critical care have reduced intensive care unit (ICU) mortality, but improved survival has not consistently translated into meaningful long-term recovery. This "survival-morbidity paradox" highlights the need to consider patient-centred outcomes beyond survival. item.description: Severe acute kidney injury in critically ill patients may require continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), yet mortality remains high. A standard CRRT intensity is 20-25 mL/kg/hr, because higher doses have not improved outcomes. item.description: This study looked at Japanese physiotherapists who worked with COVID-19 patients and found that direct contact with patients contributed to burnout, but this effect was partly buffered by appreciation and respect from patients and colleagues. The study suggests that organisational resources, such as reimbursement for care, may also play a role in burnout. Burnout prevalence was 19.4% among the physiotherapists.
